source_read: PDF, pp. 9414–9418 (all 5 pages read; Table 1 and Figures 1–3 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi)

claims.note: This source gives short-abstinence users 25% (caudate, from Table 1; the text says 26%) and 21% (putamen) below controls, inside the claim's 20–28% range. The 12 short-abstinence users are 12 of the 15 participants of Volkow 2001a (p. 9414–9415), although compared here with a different control group (11 controls, 7 women, vs 18 controls, 12 men, in 2001a). The two papers are therefore not independent evidence for this claim and should not be counted as separate studies. The protracted-abstinence group (n=10) was not significantly below controls, which bears on the claim's population ('days to months' of abstinence).

anchors.locator: Table 1; Results › 'Comparison between controls and METH abusers tested during short or protracted abstinence'
anchors.extracted: Bmax/Kd, controls (n=11) vs short-abstinence users (n=12, 64 ± 40 days abstinent): caudate 1.76 ± 0.27 vs 1.32 ± 0.28; putamen 1.97 ± 0.21 vs 1.56 ± 0.30; post hoc p<0.001 (text) / p<0.003 (table footnote). Text gives 26% and 21% lower; my recomputation from Table 1 gives 25.0% and 20.8%. Group effect F(2,30)=7.9 (caudate) and 5.5 (putamen).

anchors.locator: Introduction, last paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis
anchors.extracted: The 12 short-abstinence users are the original sample reported in Volkow et al. (2001), i.e. not a new sample; 7 women, 5 men, age 30 ± 6.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'people abstinent for a similar time (n=10)' reads as an independent group, but 5 of the 10 are the same five retested people (their second scans), so the cross-sectional and within-person findings are not independent. Suggest '10 people, including the five retested'.
claims.note: All numbers from this source checked. Within-person +19% caudate and +16% putamen (text p. 9415; my reading of Figure 2 gives about +19% and +16%). Short abstinence vs controls: text 26% and 21%; Table 1 gives 25.0% and 20.8% (26% cannot be reached from the printed table values even allowing for rounding; maximum about 25.5%). Protracted vs controls: 5.1% and 8.6% below (printed 5% and 9%). Editors' calculation recomputed from Table 1: standardized differences −0.32 (Hedges g −0.31; 95% CI −1.18 to 0.54) for caudate and −0.60 (g −0.57; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.28) for putamen: same as the claim's 'about −0.3 and −0.6'; the intervals do not exclude even a large remaining difference. 'Started with higher transporter levels' is significant for putamen only (caudate a trend, p<0.07); from the printed one-decimal SDs I get p≈0.05 for putamen, not reproducible exactly, plausibly because of rounding. The statement about another PET study finding no relation with abstinence does not come from this source. The participants were in a California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation programme, which the claim's 'treatment programme' covers but does not specify.

anchors.extracted: 5 users (3 women, 2 men; 29 ± 3 years) scanned in early abstinence (3 ± 1.6 months) and again at least 9 months later (14 ± 2 months abstinent); they were the 5 of the original 12 able to stay drug-free for 9 months. 5 further users (4 women, 1 man; 35 ± 3 years) scanned once after 17 ± 10 months. Users in a California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation programme with weekly or biweekly drug screens. 11 controls (7 women, 4 men; 31 ± 7 years) scanned once.

anchors.locator: Results › 'DAT in the five METH abusers tested twice'; Figure 2 (p. 9416)
anchors.extracted: K1 unchanged between scans (cerebellum 0.45 vs 0.47; caudate 0.55 vs 0.55; putamen 0.63 vs 0.63). Bmax/Kd increased +19% caudate (p<0.003) and +16% putamen (p<0.05). Figure 2: all 5 rose in caudate; in putamen one of the 5 showed essentially no change.

anchors.locator: Table 1 and its footnote; Results › 'Comparison between controls and METH abusers…'
anchors.extracted: Protracted-abstinence group n=10 (15 ± 7 months; includes the 5 retested users' second scans): caudate 1.67 ± 0.29, putamen 1.80 ± 0.35 vs controls 1.76 ± 0.27 and 1.97 ± 0.21; 5% and 9% lower, not significant. Short vs protracted: caudate 26% (p<0.01), putamen 15% (trend, p<0.10). Short (n=12) vs controls: 26% and 21% lower in text.

anchors.locator: Results › section on dropouts vs completers ('Comparison between METH abusers who dropped out…')
anchors.extracted: At the first scan, the 7 who dropped out (probably relapsed) vs the 5 who stayed abstinent: putamen 1.40 ± 0.3 vs 1.74 ± 0.2 (df=10, p<0.03); caudate 1.20 ± 0.2 vs 1.48 ± 0.3 (p<0.07); dropouts also worse on pegboard (92 ± 19 vs 67 ± 9 s) and delayed recall (8 ± 2 vs 12 ± 3 words), both p<0.05.

anchors.locator: Methods › Subjects and Statistical analysis (controls scanned once; only users retested); Discussion › 'Differences between METH abusers who dropped out…'
anchors.extracted: No control participant was rescanned, so test–retest change is not estimated. Authors concede the completers may have started with less damage and that studies comparing completers and relapsers are needed before generalizing.

claims.note: The source supports 'cannot distinguish' and 'some markers return toward normal'. It qualifies 'reversible down-regulation': the authors argue that a recovery taking longer than 6–9 months is longer than expected for down-regulation or internalization, and also discuss regeneration or sprouting of terminals. It does not address the Parkinson's pattern beyond a magnitude comparison in the introduction.

anchors.extracted: Authors list three readings of the DAT increase: temporary adaptive down-regulation, damaged terminals that recover, or increased arborization of remaining terminals.

anchors.locator: Discussion › 'Interpretation of DAT losses with METH and their recovery with protracted abstinence'
anchors.extracted: Earlier attribution to irreversible terminal degeneration is questioned by recovery data; inference from preserved VMAT in post-mortem tissue is limited because VMAT is also expressed outside dopamine neurons; recovery could reflect repair or adaptive down-regulation/internalization; the authors argue the slow time course (over 6–9 months) is longer than expected for down-regulation, and raise regeneration or branching of terminals; DAT over-expression by viable terminals judged unlikely.
DAT loss reported in users (24–30%) described as smaller than in Parkinson's disease (36% and 71%); magnitude comparison only, not the regional pattern.

claims.note: This source has no retested control group, so it cannot separate practice effects; its data are consistent with 'not established'. It does not contradict the claim.

anchors.locator: Results › 'Neuropsychological performance in METH abusers tested twice during short and protracted abstinence'
anchors.extracted: In the 5 retested users only: Timed Gait 10.0 ± 1 to 8.6 ± 2 s (p<0.13); delayed recall 11.6 ± 3 to 12.8 ± 2 words (p<0.10); no change in pegboard, immediate or interference recall (values not given). DAT change vs test change: r=0.78 (p<0.12) and r=0.71 (p<0.18). No control retest and no normative comparison.

anchors.locator: Discussion › 'Neuropsychological function did not recover with protracted abstinence', end
anchors.extracted: Authors concede that failure to find an association may reflect the low power of the small sample and call for larger prospective studies.

key_findings.correction: Data correct. Text is on p. 9415 (Results, 1st section), but Figure 2 is on p. 9416; page should read pp. 9415–9416.
Faithful to the text. Note that Table 1 gives 25.0% for caudate (1.32 vs 1.76), not the text's 26%. The n=10 protracted group includes the 5 retested users' second scans (see missed).

The r=0.92 result is stated in the text on p. 9415 (Results, 1st section, right column); Figure 3B is on p. 9416. Page should read pp. 9415–9416. Editors' interval 0.20–0.99 recomputed (Fisher z, n=5): same.
The Discussion (p. 9417) adds a fourth option (over-expression by viable terminals, judged unlikely) and argues that the slow time course argues against simple down-regulation.

reporting_issues.note: The printed p-values match n−2=3 df (r=0.83 gives p≈0.082 with 3 df but p≈0.041 with 4 df; r=0.88 gives p≈0.049 with 3 df), so the df label looks like a misprint rather than a wrong analysis. The same df=4 is printed in Figure 3's caption.
Figure 3A (p. 9416) plots the change on an inverted axis with negative values (−0.7 at the top), which is how the negative relation appears; the coefficients are printed unsigned.
0.25 g/day here (p. 9415) vs 0.5 g/day in Volkow 2001a (p. 378) for overlapping participants.
Abstract (p. 9414) and heading (p. 9417); the text itself concedes low power (p. 9418).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall very high agreed. An extra concern for the cross-sectional comparison: the factorial ANOVA treats the short (n=12) and protracted (n=10) groups as independent although 5 people are in both.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. Also: the title and summary call the change 'recovery' of a methamphetamine-induced loss (p. 9418), presupposing that early-abstinence DAT was drug-induced and that later values are a return toward a pre-use level, neither of which the design can show.

missed: Card sample n_total=33 counts scans in the cross-sectional analysis (11+12+10), not people. Distinct participants: 28 (11 controls; 12 short-abstinence users, 5 of whom were rescanned; 5 users scanned once in protracted abstinence) (p. 9415).
Reporting issue: the factorial ANOVA (F with df 2,30) treats the short- and protracted-abstinence groups as independent although the 5 retested users are in both (Table 1 footnote, p. 9416).

Reporting issue: short abstinence vs controls is given as 26% for caudate in the text (p. 9416), while Table 1 (1.32 vs 1.76) gives 25.0%; the difference cannot be explained by rounding of the printed values.

The control group (11 people, 7 women) differs from the 18 controls (12 men) against whom the same 12 short-abstinence users were compared in Volkow 2001a; the paper does not explain the change. The two papers share most users, so they are not independent replications for the DAT-difference claim.
Minor inconsistency: Methods state paired t tests for the within-person change (p. 9415), while the Figure 2 caption says repeated-measures ANOVA (p. 9416).
